extracted.intended_audience: political theorists, constitutional designers, and informed readers interested in forms of government
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether and how democratic or mixed forms of government are practicable and stable in different social, geographic, and institutional contexts, using historical and comparative examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collection of all authority into one centre
rubrics_metrics.description: The author's examination of Mr. Turgot's phrase 'collecting all authority into one centre, the nation' and the difficulty of understanding what is meant when the 'centre' is the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between the nation as a formal sovereign and the operative 'centre' of authority (e.g. the whole people vs the majority vs an elected assembly). The passage argues that claiming 'the nation' as the centre without an intermediary leaves you where you began (authority = nation), and that an operative centre typically becomes the majority or an assembly. Use this test to judge claims of 'national' sovereignty: who actually makes and executes laws in practice?

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicability of a simple/direct democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertion that 'A simple and perfect democracy never yet existed among men.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat claims of direct (whole-people) democracy skeptically: test logistical feasibility (can the whole people assemble? how long would it take?), and examine historical precedent — the author finds no successful example beyond very small communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and logistics required for popular assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical question: 'Where is the plain large enough to hold them; and what are the means, and how long would be the time, necessary to assemble them together?' (example of Virginia, half a million souls scattered over territory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether geography, population size, and dispersal make direct popular decision-making feasible. Large, scattered populations make direct assembly impractical; representative mechanisms or delegated centres of authority become necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers (legislative, executive, judicial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that annual administration (e.g. in the United States) is 'divided into executive, legislative, and judicial powers' and that even very democratic societies still separate functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a government's powers are divided among distinct organs and whether that division is explicit and functional. Use the presence of separate executive officers, independent judiciary, and a legislature as a criterion for avoiding concentration of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of the legislature into monarchical, aristocratical, and democratical branches
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim that 'the legislature itself is divided into monarchical, aristocratical, and democratical branches' in many well-functioning mixed systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for internal legislative structure that balances different social orders (e.g., a governor/monarchical element, a senate/aristocratic element, and a popular assembly). The author treats such division as a sought equilibrium that protects liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation by property/house versus representation of persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: the arengo's 'original representation ... of houses, that is, of property, rather than of the persons of the citizens,' which made representation unequal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether representation mechanisms are based on property units or on equal-person suffrage. Property-based representation tends to exclude non-proprietors and produce inequality; this criterion examines the basis of representation and its implications for equality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility and composition rules for office (age, nobility, property, lineage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous constitutional constraints cited (half nobles in council, minimum age of five-and-twenty, two-thirds confirmation, 'no son can be admitted during the life of his father', Biscay deputies must be nobles, worth a thousand ducats, no traders, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize formal eligibility requirements and composition rules: they may create a contracted aristocracy beneath a democratic veneer. Use these rules to judge whether offices are genuinely open or effectively hereditary/oligarchic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term limits and rotation to prevent concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of short terms and rotation: the capitaneos chosen every six months (office never to be continued to the same persons twice successively), and other limited term appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess frequency of elections and explicit rotation provisions. Short terms and bans on immediate reappointment reduce the risk of personal power consolidation; note exceptions where individuals nevertheless serve repeatedly over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial impartiality through outsider appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice in St. Marino of appointing 'always a foreigner' as commissary who 'must be a doctor of law, and a man of known integrity' and is maintained out of public stock for three years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the judiciary or key judicial officers are insulated from local factional pressures (e.g., by selecting outsiders or by tenure/security measures). Such devices are presented as deliberate checks to make judicial power an effective check on other branches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsion and penalties to secure civic participation
rubrics_metrics.description: The law obliging attendance at the arengo under penalty (e.g., a fine for absence; in St. Marino a fine of one penny is noted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether civic participation is voluntary or enforced, and the consequences of absenteeism. The author warns that nonattendance opens the door to active minorities and factional manipulation, so attendance rules are judged important to democratic health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small population intimacy as a guard against tyranny
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that 'in so small a State, where every man personally knows every other, ... it is scarcely possible that any thing like tyranny or cruelty can take place.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use community size/social intimacy as a criterion: small, closely-knit polities can rely more on reputational and direct social controls, while large anonymous populations require stronger institutional checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geography and defensibility supporting liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated examples (St. Marino on a high craggy mountain with one road; Biscay's rugged mountains and walled towns) showing physical isolation/defensibility preserves independence and liberties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how physical terrain, compactness, and defensibility affect a polity's ability to remain autonomous and resist external imposition. Small, defensible territories can sustain unusual constitutional arrangements that would not scale elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military preparedness and armed populace as a means of preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that 'All that are capable of bearing arms, are exercised, and ready at a moment's call' (St. Marino) and Biscay's long reputation as soldiers and sailors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the degree to which citizen arms, militia organization, and readiness affect political independence and internal coercion. An armed, trained populace can deter external domination and enforce internal liberties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic structure and social conditions influence on governance
rubrics_metrics.description: Noted effects of poverty and simplicity (St. Marino's poverty and simple life protect liberty) and the claim that Biscay's flourishing commerce is probably due to their liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate economic patterns (poverty vs. wealth, commerce, absence of luxury) for their impact on political behavior. Low luxury and subsistence lifestyles can reduce corruption and factional ambition; commerce and wealth may interact with liberty in complex ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional complexity and confederation shapes (cantons, leagues) prevent pure democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that Swiss cantons and the Grisons' 'Three Leagues' have very complicated governments and are mixtures of the three powers, so there is 'neither a simple democracy, nor a simple aristocracy' among them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims of 'democracy' in federations/confederations, analyze the multilayered institutional arrangements (local councils, leagues, general diets) — complexity usually implies mixed government rather than pure popular rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Susceptibility to division and factional secession
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of Appenzel dividing into Inner and Outer after violent contest; Biscay's disposition to division (Guipuscoa and Alaba breaking off) and general warning that democracies are disposed to division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the polity's vulnerability to internal splits: look for historical precedents of secession or partition, and constitutional or social fault-lines that enable factions to cleave the polity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voting procedures in federations and equality of voices across subunits
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Grisons the three leagues 'count the voices without distinction of leagues' even though one league has more deputies than another; the commons elect and instruct deputies for the general diet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze how votes are aggregated across subunits (per capita, per unit, weighted equally). The aggregation rule affects whether federated units act as a single body or maintain sectional dominance; check whether deputies are instructed and how representation translates into collective decision-making.
